drills.los_text: describe the structure of the CFA Institute Professional Conduct Program and the disciplinary review process for the enforcement of the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct
drills.reading_name: Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct

questions.stem: Enforcement of the CFA Institute Code and Standards is most likely the responsibility of:

options.A: the Disciplinary Review Committee, independently of the Board.
options.B: an external law firm retained by the Board.
options.C: the Professional Conduct group and the Disciplinary Review Committee.

rationales.A: The CFA Institute Board of Governors maintains oversight of and responsibility for the Professional Conduct group, and enforcement is shared between that group and the Disciplinary Review Committee (DRC). The DRC therefore neither acts alone nor operates free of the Board; it also partners with Professional Conduct staff to establish and review professional conduct policies.
rationales.B: Investigations are carried out by standing internal Professional Conduct (PC) staff, who investigate allegations of misconduct by members and candidates, and hearing panels are staffed by volunteer CFA charterholders on the Disciplinary Review Committee. Enforcement is not outsourced to external counsel.
rationales.C: All CFA Institute members and candidates for the CFA and CIPM designations are required to comply with the Code and Standards. The CFA Institute Board of Governors maintains oversight and responsibility for the Professional Conduct (PC) group, which, in conjunction with the Disciplinary Review Committee (DRC), is responsible for enforcement of the Code and Standards. The PC staff investigates allegations of misconduct by members and candidates. The DRC is a volunteer committee of CFA charterholders who serve on hearing panels to review misconduct allegations and impose sanctions for violations of the Code and Standards. The DRC also partners with PC staff to establish and review professional conduct policies.

questions.stem: The basic structure for enforcing the CFA Institute Code and Standards is most likely provided by:

options.A: national securities regulators acting for CFA Institute.
options.B: the Standards of Practice Handbook.
options.C: the CFA Institute Bylaws and Rules of Procedure.

rationales.A: Enforcement of the Code and Standards is a private professional conduct process of CFA Institute, governed by its own Bylaws and Rules of Procedure. It is not delegated government regulation carried out by national securities regulators on the organization's behalf.
rationales.B: The Standards of Practice Handbook provides guidance on interpreting and applying the Code and Standards, but it is the CFA Institute Bylaws and Rules of Procedure that form the enforcement structure.
rationales.C: The CFA Institute Bylaws and Rules of Procedure (Rules of Procedure) form the basic structure for enforcing the Code and Standards. They establish the procedural framework for investigations, hearings, sanctions, and other disciplinary matters.

questions.stem: A Professional Conduct investigation is most likely to arise from:

options.A: a member's self-disclosure on the annual Professional Conduct Statement.
options.B: a regulatory referral, but never a written complaint or media report.
options.C: self-disclosure alone, and from no other source.

rationales.A: Professional conduct investigations arise from a number of sources. First, members and candidates must self-disclose on the annual Professional Conduct Statement all matters that question their professional conduct, such as involvement in civil litigation or a criminal investigation, or being the subject of a written complaint. Second, written complaints received by Professional Conduct staff can bring about an investigation. Third, CFA Institute staff may become aware of questionable conduct by a member or candidate through the media, regulatory notices, or another public source. Lastly, CFA Institute works with testing centers, conducts analyses of scores and exam materials after exams, and monitors online and social media to detect potential misconduct, including disclosure of confidential exam information.
rationales.B: Written complaints received by Professional Conduct staff, and questionable conduct that staff learn of through the media, regulatory notices, or another public source, are explicitly recognized triggers of an inquiry. Investigations are therefore not confined to regulatory referrals.
rationales.C: Self-disclosure on the annual Professional Conduct Statement is only one of four sources. Written complaints, the media and other public sources, and exam-related monitoring, including analyses of scores and exam materials and monitoring of online and social media, also initiate inquiries.

questions.stem: On the annual Professional Conduct Statement, members and candidates are most likely required to:

options.A: disclose criminal convictions only.
options.B: disclose all matters that question their professional conduct.
options.C: disclose nothing, as completion is voluntary.

rationales.A: The Statement reaches all matters that question professional conduct, which includes involvement in civil litigation or a criminal investigation and being the subject of a written complaint, not only criminal convictions.
rationales.B: Members and candidates must self-disclose on the annual Professional Conduct Statement all matters that question their professional conduct, such as involvement in civil litigation or a criminal investigation or being the subject of a written complaint. This self-disclosure requirement is one of the four primary sources of professional conduct investigations.
rationales.C: Self-disclosure on the annual Professional Conduct Statement is mandatory for members and candidates, not voluntary, and it is one of the primary sources from which professional conduct investigations arise.

questions.stem: Professional Conduct inquiries are most likely to:

options.A: exclude media reports, which are unverified.
options.B: arise from the media, regulatory notices, or another public source.
options.C: require a regulator referral accompanied by formal findings.

rationales.A: CFA Institute staff may become aware of questionable conduct by a member or candidate through the media, regulatory notices, or another public source, so media reports are a recognized source of inquiries rather than an excluded one.
rationales.B: CFA Institute staff may become aware of questionable conduct by a member or candidate through the media, regulatory notices, or another public source. This is one of the four sources of professional conduct investigations, and an inquiry can be initiated in response to information provided by the media.
rationales.C: A public source need not be a regulator referral carrying formal findings. Information from the media or another public source is enough for staff to become aware of questionable conduct and prompt an inquiry.

questions.stem: CFA Institute's monitoring for exam-related misconduct is most likely to:

options.A: extend to post-exam score analysis and social media monitoring.
options.B: end when the testing session closes.
options.C: exclude online and social media activity.

rationales.A: CFA Institute works with testing centers, conducts analyses of scores and exam materials after exams, and monitors online and social media to detect potential misconduct, including the disclosure of confidential exam information. This exam-integrity work is one of the sources from which professional conduct investigations arise, alongside self-disclosure on the annual Professional Conduct Statement, written complaints received by Professional Conduct staff, and reports of member conduct from the media and other outside sources. Because some irregularities can only be identified by comparing results and materials across candidates, that analysis necessarily takes place after the testing session has closed.
rationales.B: Monitoring does not end when the testing session closes. Analyses of scores and exam materials are conducted after the exam as part of misconduct detection, and patterns of irregularity across candidates can only be identified once the full set of results and materials is available for comparison.
rationales.C: Monitoring of online activity and social media is an explicit component of CFA Institute's exam-integrity efforts. It is aimed in particular at the disclosure of confidential exam information, which is one of the forms of misconduct these efforts are designed to detect.

questions.stem: A Professional Conduct staff investigation of a member or candidate is most likely to:

options.A: rely only on records obtained from third parties.
options.B: be limited to a review of public filings.
options.C: include a written explanation from the member.

rationales.A: Professional Conduct staff is not barred from contacting the subject of an inquiry. An investigation may include requesting a written explanation directly from the member or candidate and interviewing that person, so third-party documents and records are only one of several sources the staff relies on.
rationales.B: An investigation is not confined to public filings. Requesting the member's or candidate's written explanation is a core investigative step, and staff may also interview the member or candidate, complaining parties, and third parties, and collect documents and records relevant to the investigation.
rationales.C: When an inquiry is initiated, Professional Conduct staff conducts an investigation that may include requesting a written explanation from the member or candidate; interviewing the member or candidate, complaining parties, and third parties; and collecting documents and records relevant to the investigation. The written explanation is sought from the subject directly, so the investigation is neither restricted to public records nor conducted at arm's length from the member or candidate.

questions.stem: After reviewing the material obtained during an investigation, CFA Institute Professional Conduct staff is most likely to:

options.A: close the inquiry, issue a cautionary letter, or continue proceedings.
options.B: suspend or revoke the member's use of the CFA designation.
options.C: refer every inquiry to a Disciplinary Review Committee panel.

rationales.A: Upon reviewing the material obtained during the investigation, Professional Conduct staff may conclude the inquiry with no disciplinary sanction, issue a cautionary letter, or continue proceedings to discipline the member or candidate. If the staff believes a violation of the Code and Standards has occurred, the member or candidate has the opportunity to reject or accept any charges and the proposed sanction.
rationales.B: This confuses the roles within the Professional Conduct Program. Professional Conduct staff may propose charges and a sanction, which the member or candidate is free to accept, but imposing a sanction in a contested matter is the task of a Disciplinary Review Committee hearing panel rather than of staff acting alone.
rationales.C: This misreads the process. Professional Conduct staff may conclude an inquiry with no sanction or issue a cautionary letter, so not every inquiry goes further, and a matter reaches a Disciplinary Review Committee panel only once the member or candidate rejects the proposed charges and sanction.

questions.stem: If a member or candidate does not accept the charges and proposed sanction, the matter is most likely:

options.A: referred to a panel of Disciplinary Review Committee members.
options.B: referred to the civil courts.
options.C: resolved by automatic suspension.

rationales.A: If the member or candidate does not accept the charges and proposed sanction, the matter is referred to a panel composed of Disciplinary Review Committee members. DRC panels evaluate materials and presentations from Professional Conduct staff and from the member or candidate. In contested matters, the panel's task is to determine whether the member or candidate violated the Code and Standards or testing policies and, if so, what sanction should be imposed. DRC panels also review matters in which members and candidates agree to the proposed charges and sanction, to ensure that the findings are reasonable.
rationales.B: Enforcement of the Code and Standards is a private professional process internal to CFA Institute rather than a judicial one. Rejecting the charges refers the matter to a hearing panel composed of Disciplinary Review Committee members, not to the civil courts.
rationales.C: Rejection triggers panel review, not an automatic sanction. The Disciplinary Review Committee panel first determines whether the member or candidate violated the Code and Standards or testing policies and only then decides what sanction, if any, should be imposed.

questions.stem: The sanctions CFA Institute may impose on a member or candidate are most likely to include:

options.A: public censure, suspension, and revocation of the designation.
options.B: private cautionary letters only.
options.C: monetary fines.

rationales.A: Sanctions imposed by CFA Institute may have significant consequences. They include public censure, suspension of membership and of the use of the CFA designation, and revocation of membership and of the right to use the CFA designation. Candidates enrolled in the CFA Program who have violated the Code and Standards or testing policies may be suspended or prohibited from further participation in the program.
rationales.B: This overlooks that the available sanctions include public censure and the suspension or revocation of membership and of the right to use the CFA designation. A cautionary letter is one outcome Professional Conduct staff may choose at the end of an inquiry, not the limit of the sanctions CFA Institute can impose.
rationales.C: This reflects the misconception that the Professional Conduct Program levies fines. The sanctions are professional rather than financial: public censure, suspension, and revocation, together with suspension from or prohibition of further participation in the CFA Program for candidates.

questions.stem: The CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct are most likely to:

options.A: allow a firm to claim verified compliance.
options.B: apply to individual members and CFA and CIPM candidates.
options.C: bind any firm that employs CFA charterholders.

rationales.A: The prescribed compliance statement expressly notes that the claim 'has not been verified by CFA Institute.' A party may state that it claims compliance, but it may not represent that its compliance has been verified.
rationales.B: The Code and Standards apply to individual members of CFA Institute and candidates for the CFA and CIPM designations. CFA Institute does encourage firms to adopt the Code and Standards as part of their own code of ethics, and those who claim compliance should fully understand the requirements of each principle. Once a party, whether a nonmember or a firm, ensures that its code of ethics meets the principles of the Code and Standards, that party should make the following statement whenever claiming compliance: '[Insert name of party] claims compliance with the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct. This claim has not been verified by CFA Institute.'
rationales.C: The Code and Standards apply to individual members and candidates. Firms are encouraged, not required, to adopt them as part of their own code of ethics, so employing charterholders does not automatically bind a firm to them.

questions.stem: The CFA Institute Asset Manager Code is most likely:

options.A: limited to individual charterholders.
options.B: mandatory for firms that employ charterholders.
options.C: intended to help asset managers comply with regulations on codes of ethics.

rationales.A: The Asset Manager Code is designed for adoption by firms, that is, by asset managers, rather than by individuals. It is the Code and Standards that are aimed at individual investment professionals who are members of CFA Institute or candidates for its designations.
rationales.B: Adoption of the Asset Manager Code is voluntary. Employing CFA charterholders obliges those individuals to follow the Code and Standards, but it does not make the firm-level Asset Manager Code mandatory for their employer.
rationales.C: CFA Institute has also published the CFA Institute Asset Manager Code, which is designed in part to help asset managers comply with regulations mandating codes of ethics for investment advisers. Whereas the Code and Standards are aimed at individual investment professionals who are members of CFA Institute or candidates for CFA Institute designations, the Asset Manager Code applies to firms. It provides specific, practical guidelines for asset managers in six areas: loyalty to clients, the investment process, trading, compliance, performance, and disclosure.

questions.stem: The CFA Institute Standards of Practice Council (SPC) is most likely:

options.A: a volunteer group of charterholders from many different markets.
options.B: a committee that convenes hearing panels and imposes sanctions.
options.C: a body of paid staff attorneys that prosecutes violations.

rationales.A: The CFA Institute Standards of Practice Council is a group consisting of CFA charterholder volunteers from many different markets, charged with maintaining and interpreting the Code and Standards and ensuring that they are effective. The SPC draws its membership from a broad spectrum of organizations in the securities field, including brokers, investment advisers, banks, and insurance companies. It continually evaluates the Code and Standards, as well as the guidance in the Standards of Practice Handbook, to ensure that they are representative of high standards of professional conduct, relevant to the changing nature of the investment profession, globally applicable, and sufficiently comprehensive, practical, and specific.
rationales.B: Adjudicating contested matters and imposing sanctions is the role of the Disciplinary Review Committee and the hearing panels drawn from it, not of the SPC, whose charge is to maintain and interpret the Code and Standards and keep them effective.
rationales.C: This confuses the SPC with the Professional Conduct staff. The SPC is a volunteer body of charterholders that maintains and interprets the Code and Standards; investigating potential violations and bringing charges is the work of Professional Conduct staff.

questions.stem: The Standards of Practice Handbook is most likely to:

options.A: set out the procedures for investigations, hearings, and sanctions.
options.B: impose binding rules that supersede local securities law.
options.C: guide practitioners facing day-to-day ethical dilemmas.

rationales.A: The procedures governing investigations, hearings, and disciplinary sanctions are established by the CFA Institute Bylaws and the Rules of Procedure for proceedings related to professional conduct, not by the Handbook, which is a source of ethical guidance rather than of procedural rules.
rationales.B: The Handbook provides ethical guidance and does not constitute binding law or supersede legal and regulatory requirements. Members and candidates remain subject to applicable law, and where that law is stricter than the Code and Standards they must follow the stricter requirement.
rationales.C: The Standards of Practice Handbook provides guidance to the people who grapple with real ethical dilemmas in the investment profession on a daily basis. It addresses the professional intersection where theory meets practice and where the concept of ethical behavior crosses from the abstract to the concrete. The Handbook is written for a diverse global audience of CFA Institute members and investment professionals who are navigating ambiguous ethical situations and seeking to understand the nature of their responsibilities to each other, to existing and potential clients, and to the broader financial markets.

questions.stem: Ethics is best described as:

options.A: a set of principles guiding behavior that affects others.
options.B: compliance with applicable laws and regulations.
options.C: maximization of client wealth within legal limits.

rationales.A: Ethics can be defined as a set of principles or rules of conduct that provide guidance for our behavior when it affects others. Widely acknowledged fundamental ethical principles include honesty, fairness, diligence, and care and respect for others. Ethical conduct follows those principles and balances self-interest with both the direct and the indirect consequences of that behavior for other people.
rationales.B: Ethics is broader than law, and legal compliance is neither necessary nor sufficient for ethical conduct. Conduct can satisfy every applicable rule and still fail the principles of honesty, fairness, diligence, and care and respect for others that ethical behavior rests on.
rationales.C: Ethics concerns principles or rules of conduct that guide behavior when it affects others, not the maximization of client wealth subject to legal constraints. Treating law as the only limit on the pursuit of returns ignores the balancing of self-interest against the direct and indirect consequences of that behavior for other people.

questions.stem: Fully earning the trust of investors is most likely to require:

options.A: more than strict regulatory compliance.
options.B: a written code of ethics alone.
options.C: strict regulatory compliance alone.

rationales.A: Compliance with regulation alone is insufficient to fully earn investor trust. Individuals and firms must develop a 'culture of integrity' that permeates all levels of operations and promotes the ethical principles of stewardship of investor assets and working in the best interests of clients, above and beyond strict compliance with the law. A strong ethical culture that helps honest, ethical people engage in ethical behavior will foster the trust of investors, lead to robust global capital markets, and ultimately benefit society. Inevitably, some individuals will succeed at circumventing the regulatory rules for their personal gain; only the application of strong ethical principles, at both the individual level and the firm level, will limit abuses.
rationales.B: Adopting a code of ethics that clearly lays out the ethical principles guiding the thought processes and conduct a firm expects of its employees is a critical first step, but a code of ethics, while necessary, is insufficient by itself to ensure ethical behavior firm-wide. What is also required is a culture of integrity developed, maintained, and demonstrated by senior management, together with the repeated exercise of ethical decision-making skills.
rationales.C: This is the central misconception: strict compliance with all applicable regulations is a floor rather than a sufficient condition for earning investor trust. Some individuals will always succeed at circumventing regulatory rules for personal gain, so only a culture of integrity above and beyond strict compliance with the law, applied at both the individual and the firm level, will limit abuses and fully earn the trust of investors.

questions.stem: When an investment professional faces an ethical dilemma, the role of individual judgment is most likely:

options.A: critical, with laws and codes serving as guides.
options.B: replaced by prescriptive rules set out in codes of ethics.
options.C: unnecessary where laws are strictly followed.

rationales.A: Laws, regulations, professional standards, and codes of ethics can guide ethical behavior, but individual judgment is a critical ingredient in making principled choices and engaging in appropriate conduct. When faced with an ethical dilemma, individuals must have a well-developed set of principles; otherwise, their thought processes can lead to, at best, equivocation and indecision and, at worst, fraudulent conduct and destruction of the public trust. Establishing an ethical framework for an internal thought process prior to deciding to act is a crucial step in engaging in ethical conduct, and an ethical decision-making framework should provide investment professionals with a tool for following the principles of the firm's code of ethics.
rationales.B: No code of ethics anticipates every situation an investment professional will face, so a code is not designed to substitute prescriptive rules for judgment. A decision-making framework supports judgment rather than replacing it: it structures the internal thought process before the decision to act, while the individual's own well-developed set of principles remains the critical ingredient in making principled choices.
rationales.C: Laws, regulations, professional standards, and codes of ethics guide ethical behavior but do not guarantee it, so strict adherence leaves a substantial role for judgment. Individual judgment is the critical ingredient in making principled choices; without a well-developed set of principles, an individual's thought processes can lead to equivocation and indecision or, worse, to fraudulent conduct and destruction of the public trust.

questions.stem: In promoting ethical behavior among a firm's employees, a culture of integrity is most likely:

options.A: of little influence relative to individual character.
options.B: necessary reinforcement of employees' own ethical intent.
options.C: established by one-time compliance training at hiring.

rationales.A: Ethical conduct is not purely a matter of individual character. An investment professional's natural desire to 'do the right thing' must be reinforced by building a culture of integrity in the workplace, and the development, maintenance, and demonstration of a strong culture of integrity within the firm by senior management may be the single most important factor in promoting ethical behavior among the firm's employees. Firm-level culture is therefore highly influential, not marginal.
rationales.B: An investment professional's natural desire to 'do the right thing' must be reinforced by building a culture of integrity in the workplace. Development, maintenance, and demonstration of a strong culture of integrity within the firm by senior management may be the single most important factor in promoting ethical behavior among the firm's employees. Adopting a code of ethics that clearly lays out the ethical principles that guide the thought processes and conduct the firm expects from its employees is a critical first step, but a code of ethics, while necessary, is insufficient: simply nurturing an inclination to do right is no match for the multitude of daily decisions that investment managers make. Professionals need to exercise ethical decision-making skills to develop the 'muscle memory' necessary for fundamentally ethical people to make good decisions despite the reality of conflicts of interest.
rationales.C: A culture of integrity is not the product of a single onboarding session. It is built through ongoing reinforcement by senior management, who must develop, maintain, and demonstrate it, and through repeated practice: professionals need to exercise ethical decision-making skills to develop the 'muscle memory' necessary for fundamentally ethical people to make good decisions despite the reality of conflicts of interest. A code of ethics and initial training are critical first steps but are insufficient on their own.

drills.los_text: explain the ethical responsibilities required by the Code and Standards, including the subsections of each standard
drills.reading_name: Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct

questions.stem: As set out in the Preamble, the Code and Standards are most likely:

options.A: fundamental to CFA Institute's values and mission.
options.B: aspirational goals that members need not attain.
options.C: applicable only to members at investment management firms.

rationales.A: The CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct are fundamental to the values of CFA Institute and essential to achieving its mission. Since their creation in the 1960s, the Code and Standards have promoted the integrity of CFA Institute members and served as a model for measuring the ethics of investment professionals globally, regardless of job function, cultural differences, or local laws and regulations. All CFA Institute members, including holders of the Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA) designation, and all CFA candidates have the personal responsibility to embrace and uphold the provisions of the Code and Standards and are encouraged to notify their employer of this responsibility. Violations may result in disciplinary sanctions by CFA Institute, which can include revocation of membership, revocation of candidacy in the CFA Program, and revocation of the right to use the CFA designation.
rationales.B: The Code and Standards are binding on members and candidates, not merely aspirational. All members and candidates have the personal responsibility to embrace and uphold their provisions, and violations may result in disciplinary sanctions by CFA Institute, including revocation of membership, revocation of candidacy in the CFA Program, and revocation of the right to use the CFA designation. Goals one may strive toward without attaining would carry no such sanctions.
rationales.C: The Code and Standards apply to all CFA Institute members and all CFA candidates, whatever their employer. They serve as a model for measuring the ethics of investment professionals globally, regardless of job function, cultural differences, or local laws and regulations, so their reach is not limited to members employed by investment management firms.

questions.stem: The first principle of the Code of Ethics is most likely to require:

options.A: ethical conduct toward clients alone.
options.B: ethical conduct toward clients, the public, employers, employees, and colleagues.
options.C: ethical conduct toward employers ahead of clients.

rationales.A: The first principle names far more than clients. It requires members and candidates to act with integrity, competence, diligence, and respect and in an ethical manner with the public, clients, prospective clients, employers, employees, colleagues in the investment profession, and other participants in the global capital markets, so its scope is not confined to conduct toward clients.
rationales.B: The first principle of the Code of Ethics requires members and candidates to act with integrity, competence, diligence, and respect and in an ethical manner with the public, clients, prospective clients, employers, employees, colleagues in the investment profession, and other participants in the global capital markets.
rationales.C: The first principle requires integrity and ethical conduct toward the public, clients, prospective clients, employers, employees, colleagues, and other market participants; it establishes no ranking that favors the employer. Client interests and market integrity come before personal or employer advantage, and the second principle states that priority directly by placing the integrity of the investment profession and the interests of clients above one's own personal interests.

questions.stem: The second principle of the Code of Ethics is most likely to require members to place:

options.A: employer interests above the integrity of the profession.
options.B: the profession's integrity and client interests above personal interests.
options.C: personal and firm interests above client interests.

rationales.A: The second principle places the integrity of the investment profession and the interests of clients above one's own personal interests. It does not subordinate the integrity of the profession to the interests of an employer; that ordering inverts the principle, which exists precisely so that professional integrity is not traded away for the benefit of whoever is paying.
rationales.B: The second principle of the Code of Ethics requires members and candidates to place the integrity of the investment profession and the interests of clients above their own personal interests.
rationales.C: Client interests and the integrity of the investment profession must come before personal interests, and personal interests include one's own reputation and the firm's profitability. Ranking those ahead of clients reverses the ordering the second principle requires.

questions.stem: The third principle of the Code of Ethics is most likely to require:

options.A: return maximization regardless of the care exercised.
options.B: judgment subordinated to a research committee's consensus.
options.C: reasonable care and independent professional judgment.

rationales.A: The third principle addresses the care and judgment brought to professional work, not a guaranteed investment outcome. It requires reasonable care and independent professional judgment when conducting investment analysis, making investment recommendations, taking investment actions, and engaging in other professional activities. No principle of the Code promises return maximization, and none excuses a lack of reasonable care in pursuit of returns.
rationales.B: Independent professional judgment is exactly what the third principle requires, so it cannot be surrendered to the consensus view of a firm's research committee. Reasonable care and independent professional judgment must be exercised when conducting investment analysis, making investment recommendations, taking investment actions, and engaging in other professional activities; a committee view may inform that judgment but may not substitute for it.
rationales.C: The third principle of the Code of Ethics requires members and candidates to use reasonable care and exercise independent professional judgment when conducting investment analysis, making investment recommendations, taking investment actions, and engaging in other professional activities.

questions.stem: The fourth principle of the Code of Ethics is most likely to require members to:

options.A: practice ethically, with no duty regarding others.
options.B: practice and encourage others to practice ethically.
options.C: report all observed violations to securities regulators.

rationales.A: The fourth principle is not limited to one's own practice. Members and candidates must practice and encourage others to practice in a professional and ethical manner that will reflect credit on themselves and the profession, so the duty to encourage ethical practice by others is part of the principle rather than an addition to it.
rationales.B: The fourth principle of the Code of Ethics requires members and candidates to practice and encourage others to practice in a professional and ethical manner that will reflect credit on themselves and the profession.
rationales.C: The fourth principle concerns practicing, and encouraging others to practice, in a professional and ethical manner that reflects credit on the member and on the profession. It is not a mandate to report every observed violation to securities regulators; the obligation it creates runs to the quality of practice, one's own and that of others.

questions.stem: The fifth principle of the Code of Ethics is most likely to require members to promote:

options.A: capital market integrity and viability for society's benefit.
options.B: the investment industry's growth and profitability.
options.C: capital market integrity for CFA Institute members' benefit.

rationales.A: The fifth principle of the Code of Ethics requires members and candidates to promote the integrity and viability of the global capital markets for the ultimate benefit of society. The closing phrase is part of the principle and reflects the role that capital markets play in society as a whole; a version that omits 'for the ultimate benefit of society' is incomplete.
rationales.B: The fifth principle promotes the integrity and viability of the global capital markets for the ultimate benefit of society. The growth and profitability of the investment management industry is not the stated end; industry prosperity may follow from sound markets, but it is not what members are asked to promote.
rationales.C: The integrity and viability of the global capital markets are promoted for the ultimate benefit of society, not for the benefit of CFA Institute members. Substituting members for society produces the incomplete version of the principle, dropping the phrase that reflects the role capital markets play in society as a whole.

questions.stem: The sixth principle of the Code of Ethics is most likely to require members to:

options.A: earn a set number of continuing education credits annually.
options.B: maintain their own professional competence only.
options.C: maintain their own competence and that of other professionals.

rationales.A: The principles of the Code set no specific continuing education credit count. The sixth principle requires members and candidates to maintain and improve their professional competence and to strive to maintain and improve the competence of other investment professionals; it is framed as a continuing duty of competence, not as a quantified annual credit requirement.
rationales.B: The sixth principle reaches beyond one's own competence: members and candidates must also strive to maintain and improve the competence of other investment professionals. Restricting the principle to self-improvement drops that second obligation.
rationales.C: The sixth principle of the Code of Ethics requires members and candidates to maintain and improve their professional competence and strive to maintain and improve the competence of other investment professionals.

questions.stem: The subsections of Standard I (Professionalism) are most likely:

options.A: Five subsections, ending with I(E) Competence.
options.B: Five subsections, ending with I(E) Fair Dealing.
options.C: Four subsections, ending with I(D) Misconduct.

rationales.A: Standard I: Professionalism has five subsections, listed in the Standards of Professional Conduct as I. Professionalism: A. Knowledge of the Law; B. Independence and Objectivity; C. Misrepresentation; D. Misconduct; E. Competence. The count is therefore five, and Competence is the subsection that closes the group.
rationales.B: Fair Dealing is not part of Standard I at all. It is Standard III(B), under Duties to Clients, and it governs how members treat clients and prospects when taking investment action and making recommendations. The five subsections of Standard I run from Knowledge of the Law through Independence and Objectivity, Misrepresentation, and Misconduct to Competence, and the last of them is I(E) Competence.
rationales.C: Four undercounts the group. Misconduct is indeed I(D), but it is not the last subsection: I(E) Competence follows it, which makes five subsections in all and makes Competence, not Misconduct, the one that ends the list.

questions.stem: Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law most likely requires:

options.A: Complying with local law and disregarding the Code where local law is silent.
options.B: Understanding and complying with all applicable laws, rules, and regulations.
options.C: Acquiring expert knowledge of every law to which one could be subject.

rationales.A: Local law sets a floor, not a ceiling. Standard I(A) directs that in the event of a conflict, members and candidates comply with the more strict law, rule, or regulation. Where the applicable law is less strict than the Code and Standards, or is silent on the matter, the Code and Standards govern, so a member may not set them aside merely because local law does not address the conduct.
rationales.B: Standard I(A) requires that members and candidates understand and comply with all applicable laws, rules, and regulations, including the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct, of any government, regulatory organization, licensing agency, or professional association governing their professional activities. In the event of conflict, they must comply with the more strict law, rule, or regulation, and they must not knowingly participate or assist in, and must dissociate from, any violation of such laws, rules, or regulations.
rationales.C: The duty is to understand and comply with the law applicable to one's own professional activities, not to master every body of law to which one could conceivably be subject. Members are expected to know the rules governing the work they actually do and to seek the advice of counsel or their compliance function when the application of a rule is unclear; expert legal knowledge across all jurisdictions is not the standard.

questions.stem: Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity most likely requires:

options.A: Refusing every gift or benefit, whatever its value.
options.B: Accepting any gift offered by a client.
options.C: Using reasonable care and judgment to maintain independence and objectivity.

rationales.A: A blanket refusal overstates the standard. What Standard I(B) prohibits is offering, soliciting, or accepting any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that reasonably could be expected to compromise independence and objectivity. Modest or token items that could not reasonably have that effect are permissible, although employers frequently impose stricter internal limits of their own.
rationales.B: Client gifts are not exempt. Members and candidates must not accept any gift or benefit that reasonably could be expected to compromise their own or another's independence and objectivity, and that includes gifts from clients: a gift contingent on performance, or one large enough to influence how the member treats that client relative to others, is precisely the kind of benefit the standard reaches.
rationales.C: Standard I(B) requires that members and candidates use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity in their professional activities, and that they not offer, solicit, or accept any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that reasonably could be expected to compromise their own or another's independence and objectivity.

questions.stem: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation most likely requires:

options.A: Avoiding intentional misrepresentation in written research reports only.
options.B: Correcting misrepresentations rather than refraining from them.
options.C: Avoiding any knowing misrepresentation in professional activities.

rationales.A: The prohibition is not confined to written research reports. It covers any knowing misrepresentation relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities, which reaches oral statements to clients, marketing and new-business materials, performance claims, qualifications, and plagiarized work as readily as it reaches a published report.
rationales.B: Knowing misrepresentation is prohibited outright, and a later correction does not authorize it. Prompt correction may mitigate the consequences and is expected once an error comes to light, but the standard bars the member from making the misrepresentation in the first place rather than granting a window in which one is tolerated.
rationales.C: Standard I(C) requires that members and candidates not knowingly make any misrepresentations relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities. The scope is deliberately broad: the form of the communication and the medium do not matter, and what is tested is whether the member knew, or should have known, that the statement or omission would mislead.

questions.stem: Standard I(D) Misconduct most likely requires:

options.A: Avoiding dishonest conduct on the employer's premises during business hours only.
options.B: Avoiding dishonesty, fraud, deceit, and acts reflecting adversely on professional integrity.
options.C: Avoiding only conduct that results in a criminal conviction for fraud.

rationales.A: Place and time of day are irrelevant. Standard I(D) reaches professional conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, or deceit wherever it occurs, and reaches any act that reflects adversely on professional reputation, integrity, or competence, so conduct away from the office and outside business hours is covered whenever it bears on the member's professional standing.
rationales.B: Standard I(D) requires that members and candidates not engage in any professional conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, or deceit, and not commit any act that reflects adversely on their professional reputation, integrity, or competence. The second limb is what gives the standard its reach: conduct need not be fraudulent in a legal sense to violate it, provided it reflects adversely on the member's reputation, integrity, or competence.
rationales.C: No conviction, and no criminal charge, is required. An act that reflects adversely on professional reputation, integrity, or competence violates Standard I(D) whether or not any legal proceeding follows, and conversely the standard is not a general morality clause: personal conduct unrelated to professional reputation, integrity, or competence falls outside it.

questions.stem: Standard I(E) Competence most likely requires:

options.A: Maintaining the competence necessary to fulfill professional responsibilities.
options.B: Completing a minimum number of continuing education hours each year.
options.C: Holding the CFA charter before providing investment analysis or advice.

rationales.A: Standard I(E) requires that members and candidates act with and maintain the competence necessary to fulfill their professional responsibilities. Competence is measured against the responsibilities actually taken on, so it obliges a member to keep current in the areas in which they practice and to decline, or seek support for, work that falls outside what they are competent to perform.
rationales.B: The standard requires actual competence, not a prescribed quantity of continuing education. Continuing education is one way of maintaining competence, and CFA Institute encourages it, but Standard I(E) sets no mandatory annual hour requirement and hours logged would not excuse a member who lacked the competence the engagement demanded.
rationales.C: The charter is not a precondition. Standard I(E) applies to members and candidates alike and asks for the competence necessary for one's own professional responsibilities; it does not restrict investment analysis or advice to charterholders, and holding the charter would not by itself satisfy the standard in an area where the member was not competent.

questions.stem: The subsections of Standard II (Integrity of Capital Markets) are most likely:

options.A: Three subsections: Material Nonpublic Information, Market Manipulation, and Fair Dealing.
options.B: Two subsections: Material Nonpublic Information and Market Manipulation.
options.C: One subsection: Material Nonpublic Information.

rationales.A: Standard II has only two subsections, so three overcounts it, and the extra item named belongs elsewhere: Fair Dealing is Standard III(B), under Duties to Clients, where it governs the treatment of clients and prospects in investment actions and recommendations rather than the integrity of the market as a whole.
rationales.B: The Standards of Professional Conduct list Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets with two subsections, II(A) Material Nonpublic Information and II(B) Market Manipulation. The pairing is logical: one addresses trading on, or passing on, information the market does not have, and the other addresses distorting the prices or volumes the market does see.
rationales.C: One undercounts the group. Material Nonpublic Information is II(A), but it is not the whole of Standard II: II(B) Market Manipulation sits alongside it, bringing the total to two.

questions.stem: Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information most likely requires:

options.A: Disclosing to the employer any trade based on material nonpublic information.
options.B: Refraining from acting only on information obtained directly from insiders.
options.C: Refraining from acting, or causing others to act, on material nonpublic information.

rationales.A: Acting on material nonpublic information is prohibited, and telling the employer about the trade does not cure the violation. Disclosure to a supervisor or compliance officer is the right response to coming into possession of such information, because it allows the firm to restrict the security and apply its firewalls, but it is not a licence to trade.
rationales.B: The source of the information is irrelevant. Possession of information that is both material and nonpublic triggers the prohibition however it was acquired, whether from a company insider, a supplier or customer, an overheard conversation, a misdirected document, or inadvertent disclosure by the issuer. What matters is that the information could affect the value of the investment and that the market does not yet have it.
rationales.C: Standard II(A) requires that members and candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information. The second limb matters as much as the first: passing the information along, or steering another person's trade, violates the standard just as trading on one's own account does, even where the member takes no position.

questions.stem: Standard II(B) Market Manipulation most likely requires:

options.A: Avoiding practices that distort prices or inflate volume with intent to mislead.
options.B: Avoiding any trading strategy that moves market prices, whatever the intent.
options.C: Avoiding the spread of false rumors, but not transaction-based manipulation.

rationales.A: Standard II(B) requires that members and candidates not engage in practices that distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with the intent to mislead market participants. Both forms of manipulation are caught: information-based conduct such as spreading false or misleading statements, and transaction-based conduct such as wash trades, matched orders, or marking the close to set an artificial price.
rationales.B: Intent to mislead is the key element of the standard. Large legitimate orders move prices, and arbitrage and liquidity provision are intended to move prices toward fair value; neither is manipulation. What Standard II(B) prohibits is conduct whose purpose is to deceive market participants about price or volume.
rationales.C: Both channels of manipulation are covered. The standard names the distortion of prices and the artificial inflation of trading volume, so transaction-based manipulation falls squarely within it; false rumors are one way to violate Standard II(B), not the only way.

questions.stem: The subsections of Standard III (Duties to Clients) are most likely:

options.A: Six subsections, ending with III(F) Referral Fees.
options.B: Five subsections, ending with III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality.
options.C: Four subsections, ending with III(D) Preservation of Confidentiality.

rationales.A: Six overcounts the group, and the extra item named belongs to a different standard: Referral Fees is Standard VI(C), under Conflicts of Interest, where it requires disclosure of consideration received or paid for the recommendation of products or services. Standard III stops at five subsections.
rationales.B: The Standards of Professional Conduct list Standard III: Duties to Clients with five subsections: III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care; III(B) Fair Dealing; III(C) Suitability; III(D) Performance Presentation; and III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality. Preservation of Confidentiality is therefore the subsection that closes the group.
rationales.C: Four omits III(D) Performance Presentation, which sits between Suitability and Preservation of Confidentiality and requires that communications about investment performance be fair, accurate, and complete. With it included, Standard III has five subsections and Preservation of Confidentiality is III(E), not III(D).

questions.stem: Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care most likely requires:

options.A: loyalty to the employer ahead of the client.
options.B: loyalty to the client, with reasonable care and prudent judgment.
options.C: a guaranteed minimum rate of return for the client.

rationales.A: Standard III(A) requires members to place their clients' interests before their employer's or their own interests, so client loyalty takes precedence, not employer loyalty. Loyalty owed to an employer is the subject of Standard IV(A), and where the two conflict the duty to the client governs.
rationales.B: Standard III(A): 'Members and Candidates have a duty of loyalty to their clients and must act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment. Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their clients and place their clients' interests before their employer's or their own interests.' The duty therefore has two parts: loyalty to the client, and a standard of conduct in discharging it — reasonable care and prudent judgment.
rationales.C: What Standard III(A) requires is reasonable care and prudent judgment exercised for the client's benefit, which is a standard of conduct, not a standard of outcome. Nothing in the Standard obliges a member to guarantee any level of investment return, and a promise of a minimum return would misrepresent what can in fact be delivered.

questions.stem: Standard III(B) Fair Dealing most likely requires:

options.A: fair dealing in recommendations but not in investment action.
options.B: fair and objective dealing with all clients.
options.C: identical recommendations and allocations for all clients.

rationales.A: Fair dealing expressly covers investment analysis, investment recommendations, investment action, and other professional activities. Carving investment action out of the Standard understates its scope: the duty attaches to the trade and allocation decision just as it does to the advice that precedes it.
rationales.B: Standard III(B): 'Members and Candidates must deal fairly and objectively with all clients when providing investment analysis, making investment recommendations, taking investment action, or engaging in other professional activities.' The obligation runs to all clients and across all four categories of activity named in the Standard.
rationales.C: The requirement is fair and objective dealing, not identical treatment. Differing levels of service are permissible if they are disclosed and do not disadvantage any client — for example, a premium service tier is acceptable where it is available to all clients who wish to pay for it. What is prohibited is discrimination that disadvantages a client, such as giving a favored client an earlier look at a recommendation.

questions.stem: In an advisory relationship, Standard III(C) Suitability most likely requires:

options.A: inquiry into the client's experience, objectives, and constraints before acting, reassessed regularly.
options.B: a single inquiry at account opening, with no later reassessment.
options.C: inquiry only where the account is fully discretionary.

rationales.A: Standard III(C)(1): 'When Members and Candidates are in an advisory relationship with a client, they must: a. Make a reasonable inquiry into a client's or prospective client's investment experience, risk and return objectives, and financial constraints prior to making any investment recommendation or taking investment action and must reassess and update this information regularly. b. Determine that an investment is suitable to the client's financial situation and consistent with the client's written objectives, mandates, and constraints before making an investment recommendation or taking investment action. c. Judge the suitability of investments in the context of the client's total portfolio.' The inquiry comes before the recommendation or action, and it is a continuing obligation rather than a one-time one.
rationales.B: The Standard requires that the information be reassessed and updated regularly. A client's circumstances, objectives, and constraints change, so the investment policy statement and the underlying inquiry must be reviewed over the life of the relationship, not fixed at inception.
rationales.C: The three-part inquiry applies whenever the member is in an advisory relationship, whether or not the account is discretionary. Discretion affects how the member acts on the information, not whether the information must be gathered.

questions.stem: For a portfolio managed to a specific mandate, Standard III(C) Suitability most likely requires:

options.A: holdings tailored to each fund investor's personal circumstances.
options.B: deviation from the mandate whenever it is expected to raise returns.
options.C: only actions consistent with the portfolio's stated objectives and constraints.

rationales.A: Where the member manages to a mandate, strategy, or style, suitability runs to consistency with the portfolio's stated objectives and constraints, not to the personal circumstances of each investor in the fund. Those circumstances are the concern of whoever advises the investor on whether the fund belongs in that investor's own portfolio.
rationales.B: Only recommendations and actions consistent with the stated mandate are permitted. An expectation of better returns does not authorize style drift: investors selected the portfolio on its stated objectives and constraints, and departing from them defeats the purpose for which they allocated to it.
rationales.C: Standard III(C)(2): 'When Members and Candidates are responsible for managing a portfolio to a specific mandate, strategy, or style, they must make only investment recommendations or take only investment actions that are consistent with the stated objectives and constraints of the portfolio.'

questions.stem: Standard III(D) Performance Presentation most likely requires:

options.A: fair presentation only from firms that claim GIPS compliance.
options.B: reasonable efforts to make performance information fair, accurate, and complete.
options.C: reasonable efforts for all but brief performance communications.

rationales.A: Standard III(D) binds every member or candidate who communicates investment performance information, whether or not the firm claims compliance with the Global Investment Performance Standards. GIPS compliance is voluntary; the duty of fair, accurate, and complete presentation is not.
rationales.B: Standard III(D): 'When communicating investment performance information, Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that it is fair, accurate, and complete.' The obligation is one of reasonable effort applied to any communication of performance.
rationales.C: Brevity does not excuse a misleading presentation. A short summary is still a communication of performance information, so the reasonable efforts at fairness, accuracy, and completeness still apply; where a brief format cannot convey the relevant qualifications, the member should direct the recipient to the fuller presentation.

questions.stem: Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality most likely requires client information to be kept confidential:

options.A: unless the activity is illegal, disclosure is legally required, or the client permits it.
options.B: only while the client relationship continues.
options.C: without exception, even where disclosure is legally required.

rationales.A: Standard III(E): 'Members and Candidates must keep information about current, former, and prospective clients confidential unless: 1. The information concerns illegal activities on the part of the client or prospective client, 2. Disclosure is required by law, or 3. The client or prospective client permits disclosure of the information.' Those three are the only exceptions, and the duty otherwise extends to current, former, and prospective clients alike.
rationales.B: The duty covers current, former, and prospective clients, so it does not lapse when the relationship ends. Information learned about a client remains confidential after that client has left, and information learned about a prospective client is protected even if no relationship is ever formed.
rationales.C: Disclosure required by law is one of the three exceptions the Standard sets out, alongside information concerning illegal activities by the client and disclosure the client permits. Treating confidentiality as absolute would put the member in conflict with a legal obligation the Standard expressly accommodates.

questions.stem: Standard IV Duties to Employers most likely comprises:

options.A: two subsections: Loyalty and Responsibilities of Supervisors.
options.B: three subsections: Loyalty, Additional Compensation Arrangements, and Responsibilities of Supervisors.
options.C: four subsections: Loyalty, Additional Compensation Arrangements, Responsibilities of Supervisors, and Referral Fees.

rationales.A: Standard IV has three subsections, so a two-part listing is short by one: it omits IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements, which governs gifts, benefits, and outside compensation that may conflict with the employer's interest.
rationales.B: Per the Standards of Professional Conduct, Standard IV Duties to Employers: 'A. Loyalty; B. Additional Compensation Arrangements; C. Responsibilities of Supervisors.'
rationales.C: Standard IV has three subsections, not four. Referral Fees is Standard VI(C), under Standard VI Conflicts of Interest, not a subsection of Duties to Employers.

questions.stem: Standard IV(A) Loyalty (to employer) most likely requires:

options.A: never seeking employment with a competitor while still employed.
options.B: following employer directives even where they would violate the law.
options.C: acting for the employer's benefit and not depriving it of one's skills or otherwise causing it harm.

rationales.A: Preparing to leave an employer, including seeking other employment, is permitted so long as the employer's interests are not harmed in the process. What is prohibited is misappropriating the employer's property or confidential information, soliciting its clients or employees while still employed, or otherwise using employer resources to build a competing business.
rationales.B: Loyalty to an employer never requires unethical or illegal action. Where a directive conflicts with applicable law or with the Code and Standards, the member must follow the more strict of the applicable law and the Code and Standards, and must dissociate from the activity rather than comply.
rationales.C: Standard IV(A): 'In matters related to their employment, Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their employer and not deprive their employer of the advantage of their skills and abilities, divulge confidential information, or otherwise cause harm to their employer.' Depriving the employer of the advantage of one's skills and abilities, as related to that employment, is itself a violation, as is divulging the employer's confidential information.

questions.stem: Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements most likely requires:

options.A: written consent from all parties involved before accepting the arrangement.
options.B: verbal notification to a supervisor before accepting the arrangement.
options.C: disclosure of the arrangement after the fact.

rationales.A: Standard IV(B): 'Members and Candidates must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with their employer's interest unless they obtain written consent from all parties involved.' All parties means the employer and the party offering the compensation, and the consent must be obtained before the arrangement is accepted.
rationales.B: Consent must be in writing and must come from all parties involved, not from a supervisor alone and not verbally. Written consent exists so that the employer's agreement to the arrangement is documented and its terms are on the record.
rationales.C: Written consent from all parties involved must be obtained before the gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration are accepted. Disclosure after the fact leaves the employer unable to assess the conflict while it can still act on it, which is precisely what the prior-consent requirement prevents.

questions.stem: Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors most likely requires:

options.A: reasonable efforts to ensure that those under their supervision comply with law and the Code and Standards.
options.B: detection of violations after they occur, but not their prevention.
options.C: transfer of responsibility to whoever supervisory duties are delegated to.

rationales.A: Standard IV(C): 'Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that anyone subject to their supervision or authority complies with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards.' The duty reaches everyone subject to the member's supervision or authority, whether or not those persons are themselves members or candidates.
rationales.B: Reasonable efforts include prevention as well as detection: establishing adequate compliance procedures, seeing that they are communicated, and enforcing them. A supervisor who waits for violations to surface has not made the efforts the Standard requires.
rationales.C: Delegating supervisory duties does not relieve the member of supervisory responsibility. The member remains obliged to see that the person to whom the duties were delegated discharges them competently and in accordance with applicable law and the Code and Standards.

questions.stem: The subsections that make up Standard V (Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions) are most likely:

options.A: Diligence and Reasonable Basis; Communication with Clients; Record Retention.
options.B: Diligence and Reasonable Basis; Communication with Clients; Referral Fees.
options.C: Diligence and Reasonable Basis; Record Retention.

rationales.A: Standard V has three subsections, listed in the Standards of Professional Conduct in this order: V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis, V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients, and V(C) Record Retention. Together they cover the work behind a recommendation, what the client is told about it, and the records that evidence it.
rationales.B: Referral Fees is not part of Standard V. It is Standard VI(C), under Conflicts of Interest, where it requires disclosure of any compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services. The third subsection of Standard V is V(C) Record Retention.
rationales.C: This omits the middle subsection. Standard V has three parts, not two: Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients is V(B), sitting between Diligence and Reasonable Basis at V(A) and Record Retention at V(C).

questions.stem: The requirement that Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis places on a member making an investment recommendation is most likely:

options.A: A review of the product sponsor's marketing materials.
options.B: Diligence, independence, and thoroughness, with a reasonable basis.
options.C: A reasonable basis for sell recommendations only.

rationales.A: Diligence, independence, and thoroughness require analysis that goes beyond promotional material. A sponsor's marketing documents are selling the product, not researching it, so reading them leaves the member without the reasonable and adequate basis supported by appropriate research and investigation that Standard V(A) demands.
rationales.B: Standard V(A) requires members and candidates to (1) exercise diligence, independence, and thoroughness in analyzing investments, making investment recommendations, and taking investment actions, and (2) have a reasonable and adequate basis, supported by appropriate research and investigation, for any investment analysis, recommendation, or action.
rationales.C: The requirement applies to all investment analysis, recommendations, and actions, in both directions. A buy recommendation needs the same reasonable and adequate basis as a sell recommendation, and Standard V(A) draws no distinction between them.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients, disclosure of the nature of a member's services and their costs to the client is most likely:

options.A: Required only in the initial engagement letter.
options.B: Required for both clients and prospective clients.
options.C: Required only at a client's written request.

rationales.A: The disclosure obligation is ongoing, not confined to the initial engagement document. Standard V(B)(1) is not discharged once at onboarding: when the services provided or the costs borne by the client change, the disclosure has to be brought up to date.
rationales.B: Standard V(B)(1) requires members and candidates to disclose to clients and prospective clients the nature of the services provided, along with information about the costs to the client associated with those services.
rationales.C: The nature of services and the associated client costs must be disclosed affirmatively. Standard V(B)(1) puts the duty on the member rather than on the client to ask, and nothing in it makes the disclosure contingent on a written request.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B)(2), the disclosure a member must make about the investment processes used to analyze investments, select securities, and construct portfolios is most likely:

options.A: Nothing, unless the process is quantitative.
options.B: The proprietary detail and model code of the process.
options.C: The basic format and general principles of the process.

rationales.A: The disclosure obligation applies to whatever process is used, quantitative or fundamental. Standard V(B)(2) is written in terms of the investment processes members use to analyze investments, select securities, and construct portfolios, and it carves out no exception for discretionary or judgment-driven approaches.
rationales.B: The requirement is the basic format and general principles of the process, not proprietary detail. Standard V(B)(2) is satisfied by a description that lets a client judge whether the process suits the mandate; it does not oblige a member to surrender the intellectual property in a model.
rationales.C: Standard V(B)(2) requires members and candidates to disclose to clients and prospective clients the basic format and general principles of the investment processes they use to analyze investments, select securities, and construct portfolios, and to promptly disclose any changes that might materially affect those processes.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B)(3), the limitations and risks of the investment process that a member must disclose to clients are most likely:

options.A: Only those that have previously materialized.
options.B: All those that are significant.
options.C: Only those not already described in the fund's offering documents.

rationales.A: Significant limitations and risks of the process must be disclosed, not only those that have already come to pass. Standard V(B)(3) is forward-looking: a risk that has never yet cost the strategy anything, such as a liquidity mismatch that has not been tested, is still a risk the client is entitled to know about before committing capital.
rationales.B: Standard V(B)(3) requires members and candidates to disclose to clients and prospective clients significant limitations and risks associated with the investment process. The test is significance, not whether the risk has already been realized or happens to be documented somewhere else.
rationales.C: The member's disclosure duty to clients is not discharged by references buried in offering documents. Standard V(B)(3) obliges the member to disclose the significant limitations and risks of the process directly, whatever a fund's own documents happen to contain.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B)(4), the factors a member includes in communications with clients and prospective clients are most likely:

options.A: Those that reasonable judgment identifies as important.
options.B: All factors considered, whatever their importance.
options.C: Those that best support the recommendation.

rationales.A: Standard V(B)(4) requires members and candidates to use reasonable judgment in identifying which factors are important to their investment analyses, recommendations, or actions, and to include those factors in communications with clients and prospective clients.
rationales.B: Reasonable judgment identifies the important factors; exhaustive inclusion is not required. Standard V(B)(4) asks for the factors that matter to the analysis, recommendation, or action, and a communication that buries the client in every input considered serves the client no better than one that leaves the material factors out.
rationales.C: Selecting only the factors that support a recommendation would mislead the client. The judgment Standard V(B)(4) calls for has to be exercised objectively, on which factors are important to the analysis, not on which ones make the conclusion look stronger than the evidence warrants.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(B)(5), a member presenting investment analysis and recommendations is most likely required to:

options.A: Distinguish fact from opinion.
options.B: Present only verifiable facts.
options.C: Guarantee the accuracy of opinions expressed.

rationales.A: Standard V(B)(5) requires members and candidates to distinguish between fact and opinion in the presentation of investment analysis and recommendations, so that a client can see which parts of a communication rest on verifiable information and which rest on the member's judgment.
rationales.B: Opinions may be presented; they must simply be distinguished from fact. Standard V(B)(5) does not strip judgment out of a recommendation, which would make most investment analysis impossible to write, and a forecast or valuation clearly labeled as the member's view complies with the standard.
rationales.C: The requirement is to distinguish fact from opinion, not to guarantee that opinions prove accurate. An opinion honestly identified as such satisfies Standard V(B)(5) even when events go the other way, and guaranteeing an outcome would raise a misrepresentation problem of its own.

questions.stem: Under Standard V(C) Record Retention, a member whose analyses and recommendations rest on supporting records is most likely required to:

options.A: Discard the records once the recommendation is communicated.
options.B: Develop and maintain appropriate records.
options.C: Leave retention of the records to the firm.

rationales.A: Records must be developed and maintained to support investment analyses, recommendations, actions, and other investment-related communications with clients and prospective clients. The obligation outlives the communication: the record is what later demonstrates the reasonable and adequate basis required by Standard V(A), long after the recommendation was made.
rationales.B: Standard V(C) requires members and candidates to develop and maintain appropriate records to support their investment analyses, recommendations, actions, and other investment-related communications with clients and prospective clients.
rationales.C: The develop-and-maintain obligation is placed on members and candidates themselves. A firm's retention policy and systems help discharge it, and the records are generally the firm's property, but Standard V(C) does not let an individual treat record keeping as someone else's responsibility.

questions.stem: The subsections that make up Standard VI (Conflicts of Interest) are most likely:

options.A: Avoid or Disclose Conflicts; Priority of Transactions; Referral Fees; Additional Compensation Arrangements.
options.B: Avoid or Disclose Conflicts; Priority of Transactions; Referral Fees.
options.C: Avoid or Disclose Conflicts; Priority of Transactions.

rationales.A: Standard VI has three subsections, not four. Additional Compensation Arrangements is Standard IV(B), under Duties to Employers, where it governs gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration received from parties other than the employer that compete with, or might create a conflict with, the employer's interest.
rationales.B: The Standards of Professional Conduct set out Standard VI, Conflicts of Interest, in three parts: VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts, VI(B) Priority of Transactions, and VI(C) Referral Fees.
rationales.C: This omits VI(C) Referral Fees. Standard VI has three subsections, the third requiring disclosure of any compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services.

questions.stem: The matters a member must avoid or disclose under Standard VI(A), and the parties to whom that disclosure runs, are most likely:

options.A: Conflicts that have already impaired objectivity, to clients, prospective clients, and employer.
options.B: Any matter that could impair objectivity, to compliance staff rather than to clients.
options.C: Any matter that could reasonably be expected to impair objectivity, to clients, prospective clients, and employer.

rationales.A: Matters that could reasonably be expected to impair independence and objectivity are covered, so potential conflicts are included. Standard VI(A) does not wait for an actual impairment: a relationship, holding, or compensation arrangement that a reasonable person would see as capable of biasing the member must be avoided or disclosed before it does any damage.
rationales.B: Full and fair disclosure has to reach the parties whose interests could be affected, meaning clients, prospective clients, and the employer as relevant. Standard VI(A) also requires that such disclosures be prominent, delivered in plain language, and communicate the relevant information effectively, which an internal note to compliance does not accomplish for a client.
rationales.C: Standard VI(A) requires members and candidates to avoid or make full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair their independence and objectivity and interfere with their respective duties to clients, prospective clients, and employer, and to ensure that such disclosures are prominent, are delivered in plain language, and communicate the relevant information effectively.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(B), a member's own trading is most likely:

options.A: prohibited in any security held by clients.
options.B: subordinated to client and employer transactions.
options.C: permitted alongside client orders at identical prices.

rationales.A: Standard VI(B) does not bar personal ownership of a security that clients also hold. It establishes an ordering, not a prohibition: once clients and employers have been given priority, a member or candidate may invest in the same security for a personal account. A blanket ban on holding what clients hold goes beyond what the standard requires.
rationales.B: Standard VI(B), Priority of Transactions, provides that investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over investment transactions in which a member or candidate is the beneficial owner. The client's and the employer's interests are served first; the member's beneficial interest is served only after theirs, which is why firms impose blackout periods, pre-clearance, and trade-allocation procedures on personal accounts.
