rationales.C: Identical pricing does not cure the conflict. Simultaneous execution puts the member's order in competition with the client's for the liquidity available, which can move the price against the client or reduce the quantity the client is filled on. Client and employer transactions take priority, so the personal trade must follow them rather than accompany them.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(C), disclosure of referral compensation is most likely:

options.A: required to employer, clients, and prospective clients.
options.B: required only when a referred client asks about it.
options.C: required for cash payments, with in-kind benefits exempt.

rationales.A: Standard VI(C), Referral Fees, requires members and candidates to disclose to their employer, clients, and prospective clients, as appropriate, any compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services. The disclosure is affirmative and is made before or at the time of the recommendation, so that the recipient can assess the cost of the referral and any partiality it may create.
rationales.B: Disclosure under Standard VI(C) does not wait on a client's question. It must be made affirmatively to the employer, to clients, and to prospective clients as appropriate; a client who does not know an arrangement exists cannot think to ask about it, which is precisely the information asymmetry the standard removes.
rationales.C: The standard reaches any compensation, consideration, or benefit, not cash alone. Soft benefits and in-kind consideration — business referred back in return, services rendered, waived fees, gifts — must be disclosed on the same terms as a cash payment, because they create the same incentive to recommend one provider over another. Nothing in VI(C) exempts them.

questions.stem: The division of Standard VII, Responsibilities as a CFA Institute Member or CFA Candidate, is most likely:

options.A: two subsections, on performance presentation and program conduct.
options.B: one subsection, on conduct during CFA examinations.
options.C: two subsections, on program conduct and the designation.

rationales.A: Performance Presentation is Standard III(D), one of the Duties to Clients, and has nothing to do with Standard VII. Standard VII covers only a member's or candidate's responsibilities toward CFA Institute itself, in two subsections: VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs, and VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program.
rationales.B: Standard VII has two subsections, not one. Examination conduct falls under VII(A), Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs, but VII(B), Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program, is a separate subsection governing how membership, the designation, and candidacy may be described.
rationales.C: The Standards of Professional Conduct divide Standard VII into exactly two subsections: A. Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs, which protects the integrity, validity, and security of the programs, and B. Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program, which governs representations about membership, the charter, and candidacy.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(A), the prohibited conduct is most likely:

options.A: anything compromising CFA Institute or its programs.
options.B: opinions critical of CFA Institute policy.
options.C: disclosure of live examination questions only.

rationales.A: Standard VII(A), Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs, provides that members and candidates must not engage in any conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation, or the integrity, validity, or security of CFA Institute programs. The reach is deliberately broad: cheating, revealing or soliciting examination content, disregarding testing rules or administration procedures, and misrepresenting one's standing in a program all fall within it.
rationales.B: Criticism is not misconduct. Members and candidates may disagree with CFA Institute policies and procedures and may express those views publicly; VII(A) is aimed at conduct that compromises reputation, integrity, validity, or security, not at the holding or voicing of a dissenting opinion about how the Institute is run.
rationales.C: Examination confidentiality is one application of VII(A), not its boundary. The subsection covers any conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the designation, or the integrity, validity, or security of its programs — cheating, misrepresenting candidacy, breaching testing policies, and improper use of Institute materials among them.

questions.stem: Under Standard VII(B), the permissible practice is most likely:

options.A: appending the letters to a name after registering for Level III.
options.B: stating that the charter guarantees superior performance.
options.C: describing candidacy and the designation without exaggeration.

rationales.A: There is no partial designation and no provisional use of the marks. Candidacy may be stated only as fact — for example, that the person has passed Level II and is registered for the Level III examination — and the letters may never be attached to a name before the charter is awarded, however the reference is qualified. Registration for the final examination confers no interim entitlement to the designation.
rationales.B: The charter certifies that its holder has met the education, examination, and experience requirements and has committed to the Code and Standards. It certifies nothing about future returns, and no credential can. Claiming that holding it guarantees superior investment performance misrepresents the meaning and implications of the designation.
rationales.C: Standard VII(B), Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program, provides that when referring to CFA Institute, CFA Institute membership, the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program, members and candidates must not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning or implications of membership, of holding the designation, or of candidacy. Accurate, factual description is permitted; inflation of what the credential signifies is not.

questions.stem: The number of top-level Standards in the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct is most likely:

options.A: Seven.
options.B: Six.
options.C: Eight.

rationales.A: The Standards of Professional Conduct comprise seven top-level Standards: I. Professionalism; II. Integrity of Capital Markets; III. Duties to Clients; IV. Duties to Employers; V. Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions; VI. Conflicts of Interest; and VII. Responsibilities as a CFA Institute Member or CFA Candidate.
rationales.B: Six understates the count. There are seven top-level Standards, numbered I through VII, each divided into lettered subsections; omitting any one of the seven headings above leaves a body of duties the Standards in fact cover.
rationales.C: Eight overstates the count. There are seven top-level Standards, numbered I through VII. The further divisions within them — I(A) through I(D), III(A) through III(E), and so on — are lettered subsections, not additional top-level Standards.

questions.stem: When applicable laws, rules, or regulations conflict, Standard I(A) most likely requires a member to comply with:

options.A: the more strict of the applicable requirements.
options.B: the law of the member's country of residence.
options.C: the less strict requirement, where local regulators permit.

rationales.A: Standard I(A) provides that in the event of conflict, members and candidates must comply with the more strict law, rule, or regulation. The principle applies whenever jurisdictions or professional bodies impose overlapping but inconsistent requirements: the higher standard governs, whether it originates in local law, in the law of another jurisdiction in which the member does business, or in the Code and Standards themselves.
rationales.B: Residence does not settle the question. A member doing business across borders may be subject to several bodies of law at once, and Standard I(A) resolves the conflict by reference to strictness, not domicile — so the governing rule may well come from a jurisdiction the member does not live in, or from the Code and Standards rather than from any statute.
rationales.C: Permission from a local regulator does not license the weaker standard. Standard I(A) requires compliance with the stricter of the applicable laws, rules, or regulations, and where local law is less strict than the Code and Standards, the Code and Standards govern; a member cannot rely on lax local supervision to justify the lower bar.

questions.stem: Standard I(A) most likely requires a member who knows of a legal violation to:

options.A: await a regulatory charge before dissociating from the violation.
options.B: dissociate from the violation and refuse to take any part in it.
options.C: abstain from initiating the violation but stay on the account.

rationales.A: The duty is triggered by knowledge, not by enforcement. Once a member or candidate knows of a violation, Standard I(A) requires dissociation at that point; waiting for a regulator to file charges leaves the member knowingly associated with ongoing misconduct throughout the interval, which is itself the conduct the standard forbids.
rationales.B: Standard I(A) provides that members and candidates must not knowingly participate or assist in, and must dissociate from, any violation of applicable laws, rules, or regulations. Dissociation means separating oneself from the activity: declining to take part, raising the matter with a supervisor or compliance, removing one's name from the reports or recommendations concerned, and, if the conduct continues, resigning the position.
rationales.C: Standard I(A) prohibits knowing assistance as well as knowing participation. Remaining on the account while the violation continues supplies that assistance, however passively, and the member's continued involvement lends the activity cover that can amount to participation in it. Abstaining from the first step does not discharge the duty to dissociate from the rest.

questions.stem: In an advisory relationship, Standard III(C) most likely requires a suitability determination that is:

options.A: measured against the client's verbal preferences.
options.B: confirmed after execution, at the next rebalancing.
options.C: made against the written mandate before any action.

rationales.A: Suitability is judged against the client's written objectives, mandates, and constraints. A verbal preference may be reason to revisit and amend the investment policy statement, but until the written mandate is changed it governs, and an investment that conflicts with it is unsuitable whatever the client has said in conversation.
rationales.B: The determination comes first. Standard III(C)(1)(b) requires the member to establish suitability before making an investment recommendation or taking investment action. A review at the next rebalancing tests a position the client already holds; it is a monitoring step, not a substitute for the prior analysis, and it leaves the client exposed in the meantime.
rationales.C: Standard III(C)(1)(b) requires a member or candidate in an advisory relationship to determine that an investment is suitable to the client's financial situation and consistent with the client's written objectives, mandates, and constraints before making an investment recommendation or taking investment action.

questions.stem: In an advisory relationship, Standard III(C) most likely requires suitability to be judged:

options.A: in the context of the client's total portfolio.
options.B: in isolation, security by security against the risk profile.
options.C: in portfolio context only for concentrated positions.

rationales.A: Standard III(C)(1)(c) requires a member or candidate in an advisory relationship to judge the suitability of investments in the context of the client's total portfolio. A security that looks inappropriate on a standalone basis may be suitable within a diversified whole, and one that looks conservative in isolation may be unsuitable where it deepens an exposure the client already carries. The total-portfolio view is what captures diversification and overall risk.
rationales.B: Judging each holding on its own is the error the standard corrects. Because suitability is assessed in the context of the client's total portfolio, an individually volatile or illiquid security can be appropriate where it diversifies or hedges existing positions, while a security that matches the risk profile on its own terms can still be inappropriate for the portfolio it is added to.
rationales.C: No such limitation exists, and no size threshold switches the requirement on. Standard III(C)(1)(c) applies to every suitability determination in an advisory relationship: the client's total portfolio is always the frame, not only where a position is large enough to be called concentrated.

questions.stem: The scope of the prohibition imposed on members and candidates by Standard IV(A) Loyalty, in matters related to their employment, most likely extends to:

options.A: depriving the employer of the advantage of one's skills and abilities.
options.B: using skills and experience gained on the job after leaving the employer.
options.C: stealing the employer's physical property, and nothing beyond that.

rationales.A: Standard IV(A) provides that, in matters related to their employment, members and candidates must act for the benefit of their employer and must not deprive their employer of the advantage of their skills and abilities, divulge confidential information, or otherwise cause harm to their employer. The prohibition therefore has several limbs rather than one: taking one's skills to a competitor while still employed, sharing the employer's confidential information or records, and conduct that is otherwise harmful to the employer, such as misappropriating client relationships or firm property.
rationales.B: Skills and experience gained on the job, as distinct from confidential information and employer records, may be used after departure. What a departing member or candidate may not take and use is the employer's confidential information, client lists, files, or other property; the general human capital built up in the role travels with the individual.
rationales.C: The loyalty standard reaches well beyond theft of physical property. Stealing firm property is certainly conduct that causes harm to the employer, but the standard also prohibits depriving the employer of the advantage of one's skills and abilities and divulging the employer's confidential information, so treating property as the whole of its reach understates it.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(B), consent to accept a benefit that might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with the employer's interest is most likely required:

options.A: in writing from all parties involved, before the benefit is accepted.
options.B: in writing from the employer, with no need to involve other parties.
options.C: in writing from all parties involved, within thirty days of acceptance.

rationales.A: Standard IV(B) provides that members and candidates must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with, or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with, their employer's interest unless they obtain written consent from all parties involved. Two features of that requirement do the work: the consent must come from all parties involved rather than from a single one, and it must be in hand before the benefit is accepted. 'All parties' is broader than the employer and can include the client offering the benefit and any other affected party.
rationales.B: Written consent from the employer is not sufficient on its own. Where a grateful client offers compensation, the standard requires written consent from all parties involved, which includes that client as well as the employer, so that each party can assess the conflict with full knowledge of the arrangement.
rationales.C: Consent must precede acceptance of the benefit, because its purpose is to let the affected parties decide whether the arrangement is acceptable before it takes effect. Approaching all parties is therefore not enough on its own if the approach comes afterwards: the standard provides no cure period, and consent gathered after the fact does not satisfy it.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors, a member with supervisory responsibility is most likely required to:

options.A: make certain that no violation occurs among those the member supervises.
options.B: make reasonable efforts to ensure compliance by direct reports but not other staff.
options.C: make reasonable efforts to ensure compliance by anyone under supervision or authority.

rationales.A: The duty is one of reasonable efforts to ensure compliance, not an absolute guarantee of it. A supervisor who has established and enforced an adequate compliance system, provided training, and acted on what the system revealed has met the standard, even if a violation nonetheless occurred; conversely, no amount of good intention substitutes for those efforts.
rationales.B: The duty reaches anyone subject to the member's supervision or authority, which can extend beyond the formal reporting line to staff, contractors, and others over whom the member exercises authority. Confining the responsibility to direct reports and excluding others reads the standard too narrowly.
rationales.C: Standard IV(C) requires members and candidates to make reasonable efforts to ensure that anyone subject to their supervision or authority complies with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards. The responsibility is broader than detection: it includes creating and enforcing adequate compliance systems, training those supervised, and taking corrective action once a violation comes to light. A supervisor whose attention is confined to the detection and prevention of violations has read the duty too narrowly, because prevention also demands the structures that make compliance likely in the first place.

questions.stem: A member uses third-party research and a quantitative model, neither of which the member developed, in forming an investment recommendation. Under Standard V(A), the member's obligation is most likely to:

options.A: rely exclusively on research and models the member developed personally.
options.B: determine through reasonable and diligent efforts that both are sound.
options.C: leave responsibility for their quality with the firms that produced them.

rationales.A: Standard V(A) does not prohibit reliance on research or quantitative models the member did not build. Third-party research and tools may be used, provided the member performs due diligence on their soundness; a blanket prohibition on external work would be unworkable in practice and is not what the standard requires.
rationales.B: Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis requires members and candidates to exercise diligence, independence, and thoroughness and to have a reasonable and adequate basis, supported by appropriate research and investigation, for any investment analysis, recommendation, or action. That duty extends to secondary and third-party research and to quantitative tools alike: before relying on them the member must make reasonable and diligent efforts to determine that they are sound, which means examining the assumptions, the data, the methodology, and the rigor of the work rather than accepting its conclusions unexamined.
rationales.C: Responsibility cannot be shifted to the research house or the model vendor. A member relying on secondary or third-party research, or on a quantitative tool built elsewhere, must make reasonable and diligent efforts to determine that it has a sound basis, and the member remains accountable for the recommendation built on it, however reputable the source.

questions.stem: A manager alters the general principles of the process used to select securities and construct client portfolios. Under Standard V(B), disclosure of the change to clients is most likely required:

options.A: in the next regularly scheduled annual report.
options.B: promptly, whether or not returns are expected to suffer.
options.C: when the change is expected to reduce returns, and not otherwise.

rationales.A: Deferring the disclosure to the next annual report is too slow. A change that might materially affect the investment process must be disclosed promptly, so that clients learn of it while the information still bears on their decision whether to retain the manager.
rationales.B: Standard V(B) requires members and candidates to disclose to clients and prospective clients the basic format and general principles of the investment processes they use to analyze investments, select securities, and construct portfolios, and to promptly disclose any changes that might materially affect those processes. Prompt means at the time of the change rather than at the next scheduled reporting date: the client engaged the manager on the strength of a described process, so a material change to that process is information the client needs without delay. The obligation turns on materiality to the process, so it holds whether the manager expects the change to help returns or to hurt them.
rationales.C: Disclosure is triggered by materiality to the investment process, not by the direction of expected returns. A change to the basic format or general principles of the process must be disclosed even where the manager expects it to improve results, because the client is entitled to judge the process as well as the outcome.

questions.stem: An analyst's report states, without qualification, that a company 'will grow earnings 15% annually over the next five years.' Under Standard V(B)(5), this statement most likely:

options.A: Complies with the Standard, because the underlying analysis was thorough.
options.B: Violates the Standard, because opinion is presented as fact.
options.C: Complies with the Standard where the analyst believes the forecast and it proves accurate.

rationales.A: However thorough the underlying analysis, a forecast remains an opinion and must be distinguished from fact, for example by framing it as the analyst's expectation, projection, or estimate and by identifying the assumptions it rests on. Diligence in preparing the forecast goes to the reasonable-basis requirement of Standard V(A); it does not license presenting the result as established fact.
rationales.B: Standard V(B) requires members and candidates to distinguish between fact and opinion in the presentation of investment analysis, recommendations, and actions. An unqualified assertion that a company will grow earnings fifteen percent annually for five years presents an opinion, namely a forecast about an uncertain future, as a statement of fact. The remedy is to label it as the analyst's expectation and to disclose the significant assumptions and limitations behind it, so the client can weigh the forecast rather than receive it as settled.
rationales.C: The breach consists in presenting an opinion as fact, and it is complete when the report is issued. It therefore does not turn on the analyst's sincerity, and it is not cured by the forecast later proving accurate; an unqualified forecast that the analyst believed and that happens to come true was still presented improperly.

questions.stem: The difference between the historical and the current language of Standard VI(A) Conflicts of Interest is most likely that:

options.A: the historical language required disclosure and did not mention avoidance.
options.B: the current language requires avoidance and no longer permits disclosure.
options.C: the historical language required avoidance and did not mention disclosure.

rationales.A: Standard VI(A) Conflicts of Interest historically required members and candidates to disclose conflicts, but the language of the standard made no mention of avoiding conflicts, even though the guidance for the standard had long stated that best practice is to avoid conflicts or the appearance of conflicts. Including the option to avoid, rather than simply to disclose, emphasizes that members and candidates should avoid conflicts of interest whenever reasonably possible. Although avoidance is preferred, in the investment industry it is often not reasonable to avoid a conflict or the perception of one, and where avoidance is not reasonable the standard continues to require clear and complete disclosure of the conflict.
rationales.B: The current standard did not remove disclosure. It permits either avoiding the conflict or making clear and complete disclosure of it, with avoidance preferred where that is reasonably possible and disclosure required where it is not; a mandate to avoid every conflict would be unworkable in the investment industry.
rationales.C: The historical position was the reverse of this. The language of the standard required disclosure of conflicts and said nothing about avoiding them; avoidance appeared first in the guidance, as best practice, and only later in the language of the standard itself.

questions.stem: A manager emails a ratings downgrade to her largest fee-paying clients first and to her remaining clients the following day. Under Standard III(B), this practice most likely:

options.A: Violates the Standard where the clients informed later lose money, and not otherwise.
options.B: Complies with the Standard, because early delivery is a permitted premium service.
options.C: Violates the Standard, because recommendation changes must be disseminated fairly.

rationales.A: The unfair dissemination is itself the breach. Standard III(B) governs the process by which clients are treated when a recommendation changes, so the violation does not depend on whether the clients told the following day can be shown to have lost money on the delay.
rationales.B: Differing levels of service are permissible, but only where they are disclosed and available to all clients and do not disadvantage anyone. Early access to a change in recommendation does disadvantage the clients informed the following day, because the favored clients can trade on the downgrade first, so it cannot be offered as a premium service.
rationales.C: Standard III(B) requires members and candidates to deal fairly and objectively with all clients when making investment recommendations and taking investment action. Fair treatment does not require identical treatment, but a change in recommendation must be disseminated so that no client is disadvantaged by the sequence of delivery. Emailing the downgrade to the largest fee payers a day early gives them time to trade ahead of the rest, which is exactly what the standard prohibits; the manager should distribute the change simultaneously, or withhold action on it until all clients have been informed.

questions.stem: Under Standard VI(A), the disclosures a member makes to clients about a conflict of interest are most likely required to be:

options.A: accurate, whether or not prominently placed.
options.B: framed in technical legal language, suited to sophisticated clients.
options.C: prominent, in plain language, and effective in conveying the conflict.

rationales.A: Accuracy is necessary but not sufficient, because the standard also requires that the disclosure be prominent. One buried in a fine-print footnote fails however accurate it is: the test is whether the client is actually put in a position to see and understand the conflict, not whether the information can be found by someone who already knows to look for it.
rationales.B: Plain language that communicates the relevant information effectively is what the standard requires. Sophistication cannot be presumed of every client, and even a sophisticated client is entitled to a disclosure written to convey the conflict clearly rather than one drafted chiefly for the firm's legal protection.
rationales.C: Standard VI(A) requires members and candidates to make full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair their independence and objectivity or interfere with their duties, and to ensure that those disclosures are prominent, are delivered in plain language, and communicate the relevant information effectively. It is not enough that the disclosure exists somewhere in the documentation: it must be visible to the client, understandable without specialist knowledge, and sufficient for the client to judge the nature and implications of the conflict.

questions.stem: Under Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality, a member's duty of confidentiality with respect to client information is most likely:

options.A: owed to clients unless the employer authorizes disclosure.
options.B: owed to current, former, and prospective clients alike.
options.C: owed to current clients, and ends when the engagement ends.

rationales.A: The employer's wishes are not among the exceptions. Disclosure is permitted only where the information concerns illegal activities on the part of the client or prospective client, where disclosure is required by law, or where the client or prospective client permits it, so a member may not release client information merely because the employer authorizes or prefers it.
rationales.B: Standard III(E) requires members and candidates to keep information about current, former, and prospective clients confidential unless the information concerns illegal activities on the part of the client or prospective client, disclosure is required by law, or the client or prospective client permits disclosure of the information. Those three are the only exceptions to the duty, and the scope of the duty is wide in two directions: it covers prospective clients who never engage the member, and it does not lapse when an existing relationship ends.
rationales.C: The duty covers former and prospective clients as well as current ones, and it survives the end of the engagement. Information about a departed client remains confidential, which is why files and client data may not be taken or reused when either the client or the member moves on.
